question: According to the Massachusetts CDL Manual, why might a safe speed for a straight truck or single trailer combination be unsafe for a set of doubles or triples on a curve?
choice_a: Doubles and triples require gentler steering and slower speeds on curves, ramps, and off-ramps to prevent rollover
choice_b: Doubles and triples have smaller tires that lose traction more easily at any speed
choice_c: Doubles and triples are exempt from posted curve speed limits
choice_d: Doubles and triples have more powerful engines that make speed control difficult
explanation: The manual states that to prevent trailers from rolling over, you must steer gently and go slowly around corners, ramps, off-ramps, and curves, because a safe speed for a straight truck or single trailer may be too fast for a set of doubles or triples.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.1.1 Prevent Trailer from Rolling Over

question: In a set of doubles or triples, which trailer is most likely to turn over as a result of the "crack-the-whip" effect?
choice_a: The last trailer in the combination
choice_b: The first trailer directly behind the tractor
choice_c: The converter dolly itself
choice_d: All trailers turn over with equal likelihood
explanation: The manual explains that doubles and triples are more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles because of the crack-the-whip effect, and the last trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.1.2 Beware of the Crack-the-whip Effect

question: Why must drivers of doubles and triples allow more following distance and larger gaps before entering or crossing traffic?
choice_a: Because doubles and triples have weaker headlights than single trailers
choice_b: Because doubles and triples are not permitted to change lanes at any time
choice_c: Because doubles and triples take up more space and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly
choice_d: Because state law requires a fixed three-second following distance for all combination vehicles
explanation: The manual states that doubles and triples take up more space than other commercial vehicles, are longer, and need more space because they cannot be turned or stopped suddenly, so drivers must allow more following distance and make sure they have large enough gaps before entering or crossing traffic.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.1.5 Manage Space

question: Why does the Massachusetts CDL Manual say drivers must be especially careful driving double and triple bottoms in bad weather or on mountain roads?
choice_a: Because they have greater length and more dead axles for the drive axles to pull than other vehicles, increasing the chance of skids and loss of traction
choice_b: Because they are not allowed to use tire chains
choice_c: Because their fuel tanks are smaller and require more frequent stops
choice_d: Because their brakes are not required to meet federal standards
explanation: The manual notes that in bad weather, slippery conditions, and mountain driving, drivers of double and triple bottoms must be especially careful because they have greater length and more dead axles to pull with their drive axles than other drivers, resulting in more chance for skids and loss of traction.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.1.6 Adverse Conditions

question: What key precaution does the manual give for parking a set of doubles or triples?
choice_a: Only park in spaces reserved for single-trailer combinations
choice_b: Disconnect the rear trailer before parking in any lot
choice_c: Always park facing downhill
choice_d: Make sure you do not get into a spot you cannot pull straight through, being aware of how parking lots are arranged
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to make sure they do not get into a spot they cannot pull straight through, and to be aware of how parking lots are arranged in order to avoid a long and difficult escape.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.1.7 Parking the Vehicle

question: Under the Massachusetts CDL Manual, converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes, and how is this indicated?
choice_a: March 1, 1998; a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly
choice_b: March 1, 1998; a green lamp mounted on the pintle hook
choice_c: July 1, 2017; no external indicator is required
choice_d: January 1, 2000; a red lamp on the right side of the dolly
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have antilock brakes, and these dollies will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.1.8 Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: If a second (rear) trailer does not have spring brakes, how should you set its emergency brakes before coupling, according to the manual?
choice_a: Leave the trailer wheels completely unchocked and rely on the parking brake only
choice_b: Drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, then disconnect the emergency line
choice_c: Disconnect the service line and tap the brake pedal repeatedly
choice_d: Fill the trailer air tank using a hand pump before backing the tractor toward it
explanation: The manual explains that if the second trailer doesn't have spring brakes, you should drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, and disconnect the emergency line, which sets the trailer emergency brakes if the slack adjusters are correctly adjusted. Chock the wheels if you have any doubt about the brakes.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers, Secure Second (Rear) Trailer

question: For the safest handling on the road, where should the more heavily loaded semitrailer be positioned in a set of doubles?
choice_a: In the first position, directly behind the tractor
choice_b: In the rear position, behind the lighter trailer
choice_c: It does not matter which trailer carries more weight
choice_d: Split evenly so both trailers weigh exactly the same
explanation: The manual states that for the safest handling on the road, the more heavily loaded semitrailer should be in first position behind the tractor, while the lighter trailer should be in the rear.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: How does the Massachusetts CDL Manual define a converter dolly (converter gear)?
choice_a: A hydraulic lift used only to raise the landing gear of the front trailer
choice_b: A coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semitrailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig
choice_c: A three-axle unit that replaces the tractor's fifth wheel entirely
choice_d: A braking device installed exclusively on the tractor's drive axle
explanation: The manual defines a converter gear on a dolly as a coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semitrailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: Before backing a converter dolly under the rear trailer, how must the trailer height be adjusted relative to the fifth wheel?
choice_a: The trailer must be raised well above the fifth wheel so the dolly can be lowered under it
choice_b: The trailer must be exactly level with the center of the fifth wheel
choice_c: Trailer height does not need to be checked before coupling a dolly
choice_d: The trailer must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so it is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under
explanation: The manual instructs that trailer height must be correct: it must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers, Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: When making a visual check of the coupling between the converter dolly and the rear trailer, what should you look for?
choice_a: The safety chains hanging loose from the frame
choice_b: A gap of at least one inch between the upper and lower fifth wheel
choice_c: No space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, and the locking jaws closed on the kingpin
choice_d: The landing gear fully lowered to the ground
explanation: The manual states the visual check of coupling should confirm there is no visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel and that the locking jaws are closed on the kingpin.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers, Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: After coupling and charging the trailer brakes, how do you check for air at the rear of the second trailer, and what does the absence of air pressure indicate?
choice_a: Open the emergency line shut-off at the rear; if air pressure isn't there, something is wrong and the brakes won't work
choice_b: Check the landing gear crank; if it turns freely, air pressure is fine
choice_c: Open the fuel tank petcock; if fuel sprays out, the air system is properly charged
choice_d: Listen at the pintle hook; absence of sound means the coupling is too tight
explanation: The manual instructs to charge the trailer brakes by pushing the air supply knob in, then check for air at the rear of the second trailer by opening the emergency line shut-off. If air pressure isn't there, something is wrong and the brakes won't work.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers, Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: When uncoupling the rear trailer of a set of doubles, why do you lower the landing gear of the second semitrailer before pulling the dolly out?
choice_a: To remove some weight from the dolly
choice_b: To engage the tractor protection valve
choice_c: To raise the trailer's kingpin above the fifth wheel
choice_d: To disconnect the electrical cord automatically
explanation: The manual states that when uncoupling the rear trailer, you lower the landing gear of the second semitrailer enough to remove some weight from the dolly before pulling the dolly out from under the trailer.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers, Uncouple Rear Trailer

question: Why does the manual warn never to unlock the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer?
choice_a: It will automatically release the tractor's parking brake
choice_b: It voids the manufacturer's warranty on the fifth wheel
choice_c: The dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple
choice_d: It causes the converter dolly's antilock brake light to malfunction
explanation: The manual specifically warns to never unlock the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer, because the dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers, Uncouple Converter Dolly

question: What is the correct order of steps for coupling a triple-trailer rig described in the manual?
choice_a: Couple all three trailers simultaneously using three separate dollies before attaching the tractor
choice_b: Couple the third trailer to the dolly first, then attach the dolly to the tractor
choice_c: Couple the tractor to the first trailer using the tractor-semitrailer method, then move the converter dolly into position and couple the first trailer to the second trailer using the method for coupling doubles
choice_d: Attach the second trailer to the tractor first, then back the first trailer into place behind it
explanation: The manual describes coupling a triples rig by first coupling the tractor to the first trailer using the method already described for coupling tractor-semitrailers, then moving the converter dolly into position and coupling the first trailer to the second trailer using the method for coupling doubles, completing the triples rig.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.2.3 Coupling and Uncoupling Triple Trailers

question: When inspecting the lower fifth wheel on a double or triple combination, the locking jaws should be positioned around what part of the kingpin?
choice_a: Either the shank or the head, as both are acceptable
choice_b: The head of the kingpin, not the shank
choice_c: The shank of the kingpin, not the head
choice_d: The base plate beneath the kingpin
explanation: The manual's additional coupling-system inspection checks specify that the locking jaws should be around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks, Coupling System Areas

question: When checking a sliding fifth wheel on a doubles or triples combination, what problem should you check for regarding how far forward the fifth wheel is positioned?
choice_a: That the fifth wheel is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear, or the cab will hit the trailer, during turns
choice_b: That the fifth wheel is not positioned over the rear axle
choice_c: That the fifth wheel is not mounted higher than the cab roofline
choice_d: That the fifth wheel does not extend past the rear bumper
explanation: The manual instructs checking that the fifth wheel is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear, or the cab will hit the trailer, during turns.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks, Coupling System Areas

question: On a set of doubles or triples, what should the position of the shut-off valves be at the rear of the front trailer(s) versus the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: All shut-off valves on every trailer should be OPEN
choice_b: All shut-off valves on every trailer should be CLOSED
choice_c: Rear of front trailers: CLOSED; rear of last trailer: OPEN
choice_d: Rear of front trailers: OPEN; rear of last trailer: CLOSED
explanation: The manual's inspection checklist for double and triple trailers specifies that shut-off valves at the rear of front trailers should be OPEN, while the shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer should be CLOSED.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks, Double and Triple Trailers

question: During an inspection of doubles or triples, what position should the converter dolly's air tank drain valve be in?
choice_a: Closed
choice_b: Open
choice_c: Removed entirely during operation
choice_d: Half-open, to allow slow venting
explanation: The manual's inspection checklist states that the converter dolly air tank drain valve should be CLOSED.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks, Double and Triple Trailers

topic: Checking Air Flow to All Trailers
question: When checking that air flows to all trailers on a doubles or triples rig, what should you do at the rear of the last trailer to confirm the emergency line system is charged?
choice_a: Disconnect the electrical cord and check for sparking
choice_b: Loosen the pintle hook and check for movement
choice_c: Remove the spare tire and inspect the mounting bracket
choice_d: Open the emergency line shut-off valve and listen for air escaping, then close it
explanation: The manual describes going to the rear of the rig and opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; you should hear air escaping, showing the entire system is charged, then close the emergency line valve.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks, Check That Air Flows to All Trailers

question: When testing the tractor protection valve, at what air pressure range should the trailer air supply control typically pop out into the emergency position, according to the manual?
choice_a: Usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi
choice_b: Usually within the range of 5 to 10 psi
choice_c: Exactly 100 psi
choice_d: Usually within the range of 60 to 80 psi
explanation: The manual states the trailer air supply control should pop out (go from normal to emergency position) when the air pressure falls into the pressure range specified by the manufacturer, usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks, Test Tractor Protection Valve

question: What could happen if the tractor protection valve does not work properly?
choice_a: The trailer's landing gear would automatically lower while driving
choice_b: An air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control
choice_c: The converter dolly's antilock brakes would activate prematurely
choice_d: The tractor's fuel supply would be cut off
explanation: The manual warns that if the tractor protection valve doesn't work properly, an air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on, with possible loss of control.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks, Test Tractor Protection Valve

question: How do you test that the trailer emergency brakes are functioning after charging the trailer air brake system?
choice_a: Disconnect the safety chains and observe if the trailer rolls
choice_b: Apply the foot brake pedal firmly while backing up
choice_c: Pull out the trailer air supply control (or place it in the emergency position) and pull gently on the trailer with the tractor to check that the emergency brakes are on
choice_d: Open the converter dolly's petcock and listen for a hiss
explanation: The manual describes testing trailer emergency brakes by charging the trailer air brake system, checking that the trailer rolls freely, then stopping and pulling out the trailer air supply control (or placing it in the emergency position) and pulling gently on the trailer with the tractor to check that the trailer emergency brakes are on.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks, Test Trailer Emergency Brakes

question: How should trailer service brakes be tested during an inspection, and how are they controlled during normal operation?
choice_a: Tested and operated exclusively through the parking brake control
choice_b: Tested only by a mechanic using diagnostic equipment, never by the driver
choice_c: Tested with the hand control (trolley valve), but controlled in normal operation with the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels
choice_d: Tested with the foot pedal, but controlled in normal operation with the trolley valve
explanation: The manual states the trailer brakes should be tested with the hand valve (trolley valve), but controlled in normal operation with the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks, Test Trailer Service Brakes
